newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Snowballing S. Korean strikes drag down production.
newsitem.headline: Snowballing S. Korean strikes drag down production.

text.p: Production losses have begun to pile up at South Korean industries crippled by spreading strikes, the government said on Tuesday, but economists argued the unrest was more political posturing than a long-term economic threat.
More than 200,000 workers have joined the latest wave of industrial action calling for the repeal of a controversial new labour law.
The legislation, rammed through parliament on December 26, allows employers to lay off workers, replace strikers and hire temporary workers.
"It's more politicking and posturing than it is a real attempt to repeal certain provisions of the law," said Richard Samuelson, head of research at SG Warburg Securities in Seoul.
"While the strikes aren't going to disappear overnight, they are not going to drag on for months either. Their cause isn't nearly as justifiable as it was during the late 80's."
In 1989, labour disputes continued for nearly five months as workers fought for higher wages and better working conditions.
The trade ministry said on Tuesday that South Korea has suffered 1.18 trillion won ($1.39 billion) in lost production since the strikes started on December 26.
Lost exports were estimated at $244 million, the ministry said.
Many analysts agreed the impact of the strikes would depend on their length.

"If it was just a few weeks, a lot of goods could be sold out of inventory and they could work overtime to make up the difference," said Samuelson. "If it goes over a month, two months, there will be permanent damage that can't be recouped for the year."

Lee Hahn-koo, president of the private Daewoo Economic Research Institute, said if current strikes reach levels seen in 1989, the nation's gross domestic product (GDP) growth could decline to 5.6 percent, instead of a forecast 5.9 percent.
South Korea's GDP grew an estimated seven percent in 1996.
"But the strikes aren't going to last that long," Lee predicted.
"The workers know the Korean economy is in trouble, and they know that their wages are high enough compared to foreign countries."
South Korea's per capita income was just over $10,000 in 1995.
Average wages have risen by 15 percent annually since 1987, while productivity lagged behind at an average of about six percent.
Last year, spending on wages accounted for 10 percent of average company sales, figures from the Federation of Korean Industries showed.

"Korea has woken up with a hangover at the end of 1996 with a current account deficit of $20 billion, realising that the economy isn't doing that great. One reason is the high cost of labour," said a senior foreign diplomat in Seoul who asked not to be named.
However, the changes "still leave Korean labour law far more regulated and in favour of inflexible working practices than most developed countries," he added.
In a press conference on Tuesday, President Kim Young-sam ruled out compromise over the labour bill, angering militant unions who vowed to step up strikes.
In response, the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions said it would call out public sector unions to join stoppages that have idled shipbuilding yards and car plants.
Hospital workers and unionists at four big broadcasters joined the strikes on Tuesday.

Strikers represent just a fraction of South Korea's workforce of more than 10 million. But they are concentrated in huge industrial conglomerates, such as the Hyundai Group, which are the backbone of the export-led economy. ($1=844 won)
